```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
```

## Loading Processed Data

We load our processed dataset to create visualizations.

```{r}
# Load the processed dataset
load("22_DataSaving.RData")

# Get the 2020 values
education_2020 <- processed_data$X2020

# Remove missing values
education_2020 <- education_2020[!is.na(education_2020)]

# Check the number of values
length(education_2020)

# Create histogram
hist(education_2020,
     main = "Education Expenditure in 2020",
     xlab = "Education Expenditure (% of GDP)",
     ylab = "Frequency",
     col = "lightblue",
     breaks = 10)
```

## Summary Statistics

We start by looking at the summary statistics.

```{r}
# Summary of the dataset
summary(processed_data)
```

## Histogram

We create a histogram to look at the distribution of a numerical variable.

```{r}
# Load processed dataset
load("22_DataSaving.RData")

# Get education expenditure for 2020
education_2020 <- processed_data$X2020

# Remove missing values
education_2020 <- education_2020[!is.na(education_2020)]

# Check available observations
length(education_2020)

# Create histogram
hist(education_2020,
     main = "Education Expenditure in 2020",
     xlab = "Education Expenditure (% of GDP)",
     ylab = "Frequency",
     col = "lightblue",
     breaks = 10)
```

The histogram helps us understand how the values are distributed. We can use it to identify patterns and possible outliers.

## Boxplot

We create a boxplot to look at the spread of the data.

```{r}
# Create boxplot for 2020
boxplot(education_2020,
        main = "Education Expenditure in 2020",
        ylab = "Education Expenditure (% of GDP)",
        col = "lightgreen")
```

The boxplot helps us look at the median, spread, and possible outliers in the dataset.

```{r}
# Count available observations
sum(!is.na(processed_data$X2020))

# Check summary statistics
summary(processed_data$X2020)
```
